LionStory

Personalised children's books for the US, EU and UAE · 2019–2023

Our books won two Creative Child Magazine awards: Product of the Year 2022 and Book of the Year 2023.

On the product ops side I ran funnel analytics and located where users dropped off, we worked out solutions as a team, and I took the hypotheses through to production. The cases below are my hypotheses that won.

▸A new category: personalised books for ages 1–3~30% of salestime-to-market −60%

Project manager / product ops · LionStory

Context

The range was built for children aged 6–8, with a detailed avatar builder where parents picked every element. New books took a long time to make, and the audience was narrow.

What I did

After looking at the children's book market and competitors, I put forward a simpler product for ages 1–3 and tested it as an MVP. The new books used a lighter illustration style and whole avatars (five options for boys, five for girls) instead of the full builder. We released one book, checked demand and behaviour, and then expanded the line.

~30%of all sales came from the new category
−60%time-to-market compared with the main range

The simplified builder worked well enough that it was later rolled out to the main range too.

▸An onboarding quiz before the character builder+16%more visitors reached the builder

Project manager / product ops · LionStory

Context

The character builder, where parents set up how their child looks in the book, was the key step before purchase and the biggest drop-off. We had already moved it to one page and cut steps, but many visitors still never started it.

What I did

The funnel analysis showed many visitors never started the builder. My hypothesis was a short quiz before the builder: a few questions about the child and the book. It made the experience feel personal from the first screen, eased people into the builder and let us start collecting emails.

+16%share of visitors who reached the builder
~50%of visitors left their email, a new channel for follow-ups
▸Making paid book options visible40% → 80%orders with a hardcover

Project manager / product ops · LionStory

Context

A hardcover and a photo of the child on the back cover added value for families and margin for the business, but few buyers chose them. The options sat in the cart, and people couldn't see what they would get.

What I did

I added a live preview of the back cover with the photo, moved the photo and dedication options from the cart to sit under the book preview, and added an extra cover option to make the premium choice easier to pick.

40% → 80%share of books ordered with a hardcover
2×+more books with a photo on the cover
▸A second-book offer to raise order value+23%average order value

Project manager / product ops · LionStory

Context

Most customers bought one book. Acquisition costs left room for a discount on a second book without breaking unit economics.

What I did

I worked out the economics and designed a 45% discount on the second book. We first showed it in a pop-up after the first book was added, then moved it into the side cart so it felt less pushy.

+23.4%average order value
+20%books per order
▸A production process for new booksPredictable releasesstages, owners, quality gates

Project manager / product ops · LionStory

Context

LionStory released new books regularly, but the stages were blurred, teams overlapped, and release dates slipped.

What I did

I mapped the existing process and rebuilt it in three blocks: marketing, development, and design and file preparation. For every step I defined the inputs, the expected output, the artefacts, the owner and who signs off, and added quality gates before each hand-over. I ran the team's Scrum routine in Jira.

Result

A transparent process with clear ownership, predictable release dates and quality checks built into the flow.

Nasledie Digital

AI chat for preserving family history, with a printed book option · 2024–2026
▸15 interviews with paying customers+37%conversion to a request, new positioning

Product analyst · Nasledie Digital

Context

Conversion from interest to purchase was unstable, and the team didn't know what value customers saw in the product or what drove the decision to buy.

What I did

I ran 15 JTBD interviews of 45–60 minutes with paying customers, covering use cases, perceived value, alternatives and barriers. I also segmented users by age and geography and updated the customer journey map.

What we learned

  • People saw the product as an emotional gift for loved ones, not as a storage service.
  • The core value was preserving family history and personal memories.
  • The main barrier was doubt that the result would feel personal enough.

Result

Two new positioning hypotheses, an updated journey map and recommendations for how to communicate value. The hypothesis we launched raised conversion to a request by 37% compared with earlier versions.

▸What actually makes people buy a family-legacy productPurchase trigger foundinterviews and surveys

Product analyst · Nasledie Digital

Context

I joined to test a new direction aimed at parents.

What happened

The landing page converted well, but almost nobody went on to buy. I ran customer interviews and surveys with people who had bought, and found that their real reason for buying was different from the motivation the direction was built on. The specific findings are under NDA; I'm happy to talk through the approach in an interview.

Takeaway

Interest on a landing page is not demand. Validate with a paid step early, and talk to people who actually paid to learn what made them buy.

▸An AI greeting generator in a chat interface2 minmedian time to value

Product analyst · Nasledie Digital

Context

The main product asked a lot of users before they got a result, so many never reached it. The team wanted a faster way to show value.

What I did

I designed the conversation for an AI greeting generator: the dialogue logic, the user scenarios and the sequence of questions. I set up the key product metrics, then analysed where people left the scenario and iterated on the dialogue.

55%of users completed the scenario
2 minmedian time to value
▸Journey analysis for an AI fairy-tale builderHypotheses rankedwith RICE

Product analyst · Nasledie Digital

Context

In Skazochnik, users created a personalised fairy tale on the web. Many started but didn't finish, and nobody knew where the main barriers were.

What I did

I mapped the journey from landing to finished story, marked the drop-off points and wrote hypotheses about their causes: hard steps, an unclear result, cognitive load. I proposed changes to the scenario and ranked them with RICE.

Multifoto

Personalised fairy-tale books, new product line · 2026, project-based
▸Launching a personalised book line from zero11.4 → 4.1 daysfrom request to payment

Project manager, new product launch · Multifoto

Context

Multifoto, a photo-printing company, wanted a new category of personalised children's books made with AI illustration. This was a project role: the company needed someone to launch book production, build the sales funnel and give marketing its first data from early research and sales.

What I did

I launched the first version and built the production process, the funnel analytics in the CRM and a dashboard. The data showed the bottleneck was production (one designer and unstable AI image quality), not advertising, so I set a gate: scale only after the production process was stable. I also removed a free cover-approval step that came before payment.

5.4 → 1.5days median production cycle per book
11.4 → 4.1days from request to payment after removing the step, with no significant change in how many orders were paid

The process was handed over to the in-house team and runs without me.
